raw_response:
I am seventy this year, and I have been farming these fields since I was twenty. My old bones are not what they used to be, but my wife and I still get by, and my youngest son comes back from the factory in Handan to help during planting and the busy picking season. We have four mouths to feed in this household, and these five mu of cotton are what we depend on.

I finished middle school, so I can read the labels on the fertilizer bags and I have sat through a few extension meetings over the years. But to be honest, most of what I know comes from doing it myself, season after season. I still remember the bad year in 2013 when the bollworms came through and wiped out nearly half the crop. Since then, I do not skimp on pesticides, even when the prices go up. Better to spray one extra time than to lose everything.

This year, I will plant my cotton around April 20th, once the soil has warmed up properly after Qingming. I am using the same improved hybrid variety I used last year — guoxinmian, or something similar from the supply shop. The seeds cost me about 40 yuan per mu. Old Wang down the road was talking about some new variety, but at my age I do not have the energy to gamble. If it fails, I do not have time to recover.

For fertilizer, the extension agent keeps mentioning soil testing, but I know my own land. I put down about 100 kg per mu of compound fertilizer before planting — the 15-15-15 type from the co-op. That gives me roughly 15 kg each of nitrogen, phosphorus, and potassium per mu, which is what I have done for years. I used to topdress with urea at flowering, but fertilizer got expensive last year and my son said the plants looked fine without it, so this year I am skipping the topdressing to save a bit of cash. The compound fertilizer costs about 130 yuan per mu. Every yuan matters when you only have five mu.

Irrigation is a painful expense because the electricity meter spins fast, but cotton needs water at flowering and boll-setting or the bolls drop. I learned that the hard way during the dry year — I think it was 2002? — when I lost a third of my yield. So I will irrigate twice: once in early July and again in mid-August. That is about 40 yuan per mu in pumping costs.

Pesticides are the biggest expense after fertilizer. I spray for insects about 12 times starting from when the seedlings emerge. The bollworm is the main enemy, but aphids show up too. I also spray herbicide once before planting to keep the weeds down — hand weeding is too hard on my knees now. Insecticides cost about 100 yuan per mu, herbicide about 15 yuan, and I might use a plant growth regulator once or twice. All together, pesticides run about 150 yuan per mu.

For tillage, I hire the rotary tiller from the village co-op. Costs 50 yuan per mu. I used to plow with an animal when I was young, but those days are long gone.

Labor is mostly family. My wife helps with sowing and mixing spray tanks. I do the topping myself — about two days per mu, so ten days total for five mu. Picking is the killer. Each mu takes about twelve to fifteen days of picking spread across September and October, and you have to pick in rounds as the bolls open. For five mu, that is sixty to seventy days of family labor. If we fall behind — and at my age we usually do — I hire a few women from the next village for five or six days. They get paid by the kilo.

I expect about 520 kg of seed cotton per mu this year if the weather holds. Last year I got around 500, but the rain was bad in August. If I get 520, at roughly 2.8 yuan per kilo, that is about 1,450 yuan per mu. After taking out the roughly 400 yuan in input costs, I can maybe clear 1,000 yuan per mu. For five mu, that is about 5,000 yuan profit to get us through the winter. It is not much, but it is what we have.
